text: Examinations of specimen size eects on tensile properties were performed with and without neutron irradiation. Specimen thickness was varied to investigate the eect of aspect ratio as well as the thickness itself. Thickness dependence of yield stress, aspect ratio dependence of ultimate stress and aspect ratio dependence of ultimate strain showed good consistency and reproducibility even in heavy neutron irradiation condition. The eect of specimen size on yield stress and ultimate stress was small, but the ductility showed significant dependence on specimen aspect ratio. 2000 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

text: In studies for the development of fusion reactor materials, small specimens have been utilized to investigate irradiation eects on the mechanical properties of materials [1-12]. One of the major motivations to establish small specimen testing methods is the severe limitation of specimen space in irradiation facilities. Reduction of radiation dose during post-irradiation testing is also an important motivation.

text: Materials used were modified 316 austenitic stainless steel (JPCA) and ferritic/martensitic dual phase steel (JFMS) [13-16]. They were heat-treated to obtain plates with grain sizes ranging from 26 to 171 l m for JPCA and with ferrite/martensite volume ratios ranging from 0.32 to 0.37 for JFMS.

text: Two types of tensile specimens, S type and W type, were used. The gauge dimensions are 1 : 2 w 5 : 0 l 0 : 25 t mm 3 for the S type and 2 : 4 w 10 l 0 : 5 t mm 3 for W type. The blanks were cut from the thick plate with profiles of S and W type specimens, and they were sliced with a wire saw to obtain specimens. The ratio of specimen thickness to the specimen width (aspect ratio) was varied over a range from 0.01 to 1.

text: Yield strength is known to be thickness independent for thickness larger than a critical thickness t c ; Y [79,11,12]. The critical thickness depends on material. t c ; Y for aluminum alloys is 3-5 times the average grain diameter [8] and that for ferrous alloys is about 6-10 times the average prior austenite grain diameter [3,4]. Fig. 1 indicates that specimen width (i.e., specimen type) does not aect yield stress and that only specimen thickness aects yield stress for thickness smaller than t c ; Y. The critical thickness for JPCA was estimated to be 0.12 mm which is about six times the average grain diameter, and that for JFMS was 0.19 mm which is also six times the average ferrite phase diameter.

text: The critical thickness for ultimate stress t c ; UTS was found to be aected by specimen width in a previous work [16]. This is also confirmed in this work as shown in Fig. 2. text: Fig. 5 shows specimen thickness dependence of yield stress in JPCA and JFMS following irradiation to 44 and 70 dpa at 693 K and to 35 and 56 dpa at 793 K in FFTF. At the same irradiation temperature yield stress is not aected by irradiation dose. This indicates that yield stress become saturated following irradiation over about 35 dpa at these temperatures as shown in the test results for other steels [10]. Although irradiation tem- perature is dierent and the critical thickness for yield stress t c ; Y is di cult to be defined from present results, t c ; Y are considered to be equal to or smaller than that for the unirradiated or low-dose irradiation condition. The aspect ratio does not aect yield stress.
